deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page, 1852 Sept 22): a puzzle from the Illustrirte Zeitung asks for the 'letter numbers' x, y, z of the word 'Don' satisfying (1) xy - z = 43, (2) xz - y = 38, (3) yz - x = 178, (4) xyz = 728. Gauss then sets himself the harder variant of using only (1)-(3). From (1), z = xy - 43. Substituting into (2) gives y = (43x + 38)/(x^2 - 1). Substituting that into (3) and clearing denominators gives the quintic x^5 + 178x^4 - 2x^3 - 1990x^2 - 3292x - 1456 = 0. This quintic has the rational roots x = 4 and x = -2.

This page:

Step 1 (deflation). 'The three other roots are contained in the equation x^3 + 180x^2 + 366x + 182 = 0.' [Implicit, mine] Dividing the quintic by (x-4)(x+2) = x^2 - 2x - 8 gives exactly this cubic with zero remainder.

Step 2 (shift). Put x = p - 1. Then (p-1)^3 + 180(p-1)^2 + 366(p-1) + 182 = p^3 + 177p^2 + 9p - 5. The shift is natural because the cubic takes the small value -5 at x = -1, so the cubic in p has a small constant term and a root near 0.

Step 3 (numerical roots of the p-cubic). Gauss gives p ≈ +0.1445113 (written with overwritten digits), p ≈ -0.19553345 and p ≈ -176.94898. The next page shows how the small root was obtained. He rewrites the cubic as the fixed-point form p^2 = -p^3/177 - 3p/59 + 5/177 and iterates. He works with 7-place logarithms: 2.2479733 = log10 177, and 0.5677768 ≈ log10 3.696381. The successive values are 0.144, 0.14460, 0.144495, 0.14451, 0.1445112, ...

Step 4 (back to x = p - 1). An earlier, cruder set of x-values (-0.85659?, -1.19608, -177.94900) is struck through. It is replaced by:
- x ≈ -0.8554887
- x ≈ -1.1955330
- x ≈ -177.9489782

[My check] These refined values satisfy the root-sum relation p1 + p2 + p3 = -177 to all seven decimals. This strongly suggests the large root was obtained as -177 - p1 - p2. The other symmetric functions check too: p1p2 + p3(p1 + p2) ≈ 9 and p1p2p3 ≈ 5.

Step 5 (conclusion). As a letter number only x = +4 is admissible. Then y = (43·4 + 38)/15 = 14 and z = 4·14 - 43 = 13. In the 24-letter alphabet with I = J: D = 4, O = 14, N = 13, which spells 'Don'. [Mine] The other rational root gives the integer solution x = -2, y = -16, z = -11 of (1)-(3). This solution does not satisfy (4), since xyz = -352.
errors: The second root on the p-line, -0.19553345, is slightly inaccurate. One Newton step from it gives p2 ≈ -0.1955331 (f(-0.19553345) ≈ +2.2e-5, f' ≈ -60.1). The corrected x-value -1.1955330, i.e. p2 = -0.1955330, is right to about 1 unit in the 7th decimal. So the x-column supersedes the p-line.
The first p-value is written with overwritten or blotted digits (transcribed 0.14451426). The true root is p1 ≈ 0.14451127, consistent with the final x1 = -0.8554887.
The struck-out first approximations (e.g. -0.85659, -1.19608) were wrong or crude and were properly replaced. No errors remain in the final values beyond the last decimal.
Otherwise the algebra (deflation and shift) is exactly correct.

results.what: Elimination of z and y from xy - z = 43, xz - y = 38, yz - x = 178 to a quintic in x, then deflation by the rational roots 4 and -2 to the cubic x^3 + 180x^2 + 366x + 182
results.modern_name: Elimination / resultant, rational root extraction, polynomial deflation

results.what: Shift x = p - 1 to the cubic p^3 + 177p^2 + 9p - 5 = 0 and numerical solution of it
results.modern_name: Taylor shift (Horner-type translation) plus fixed-point iteration with logarithmic arithmetic; remaining root via Vieta's relation (sum of roots = -177)

results.what: Solution of the newspaper puzzle 'Don': x = 4, y = 14, z = 13 (D, O, N in the 24-letter alphabet)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine recreational computation: deflating a quintic and finding the real roots of a cubic numerically by standard iteration and logarithms. It is charming as evidence of Gauss amusing himself with a newspaper puzzle in 1852, but it contains no new mathematics.
